app.name: Sahn
app.description: An Islamic assistant that retrieves and cites - prayer times, the Quran, duas, zakat and more.

landing.heading: One courtyard, ten doors.
landing.body: A general assistant that answers anything, with prayer times, the Qur'an, duas and zakat built in - and an Islamic knowledge base behind it when the question calls for one.
landing.promise: Sahn does not issue rulings. Every answer on fiqh traces back to a named source and school, or it is not given at all.

composer.label: Ask the assistant
composer.hint: Enter to send, Shift + Enter for a new line

suggestions.one: How do the schools differ on combining prayers when travelling?
suggestions.two: Help me plan a week of meals on a tight budget

shell.notBuiltYet: This room is not built yet.
shell.phaseNote: It arrives in phase {phase} of the build.

chat.heading: Ask.
chat.summary: Ask anything at all. Where a question has an Islamic dimension, Sahn answers with that in view - and any question of Islamic law is answered only from retrieved sources, with the school named.
chat.notConnected: The assistant is not connected yet.
chat.notConnectedNote: Retrieval, the classifier and the citation engine arrive in phase {phase}. Your message stayed in this browser tab - nothing was sent anywhere.
chat.uncited: General knowledge, not scholarship - no source was cited for this.

errors.network: Could not reach Sahn. Check your connection.
errors.classifier_unavailable: Sahn could not route that safely just now. Please try again in a moment.
errors.failed: Something went wrong. Please try again.
errors.rate_limited: You have sent a lot of messages in a short time. Please wait a minute and try again.
errors.rate_limited_anon: That is as many messages as Sahn allows without an account. Sign in - it is free, and the limit is much higher.
errors.retrieval_busy: Sahn can look up sources a few times a minute at the moment. Wait about {seconds} seconds and ask again - the answer will be properly sourced rather than guessed.

chat.sourcesNote: Answers on Islam draw on a vetted Islamic knowledge base - the Qur'an with its translations, and sourced supplications - and every claim from it is cited. Everything else it answers as a general assistant.
chat.everythingElse: Ask about anything at all - code, cooking, careers, homework. Where a question has an Islamic dimension, Sahn answers with that in view.

finance.heading: Halal finance
finance.intro: Explanations of how Islamic financial structures work, and where scholars disagree about them. Reference material - Sahn does not recommend products.
finance.disclaimer: This is educational content, not financial advice. Sahn is not a regulated financial adviser and does not recommend or endorse any product or provider. Regulated advice for your circumstances should come from an authorised adviser; the religious question should go to a qualified scholar.
finance.sourcesNote: Sahn summarises and links out rather than reproducing these. The standards themselves are the authority, not this page.

account.heading: Your account
account.intro: What Sahn holds about you, and how to take it away.
account.exportBody: A complete copy of everything stored against your account - settings, worship records, saved conversations - as a JSON file.
account.deleteBody: This removes your account and every record attached to it: conversations, prayer logs, the qada ledger, bookmarks, fasts and zakat records. It happens immediately and cannot be undone. Export first if you want a copy.
account.deleteFailed: That did not go through. Nothing was deleted - please try again.

ramadan.signedOut: Sign in to keep your Ramadan record.

ramadan.missedBody: Days missed for travel, illness, menstruation or another reason, and how many you have made up since. Whether a missed fast is made up, compensated by fidya, or both depends on why it was missed - ask someone qualified about your own case.
ramadan.note: Your record is private to your account. Ramadan dates here are calculated from the Umm al-Qura calendar; your local moon-sighting authority decides when the month actually begins.

counsel.privacyNote: Nothing said here is saved unless you choose to save it, and anything you do save is encrypted in this browser with a passphrase only you hold. Sahn is not a therapist or a scholar - for a ruling, or for care, speak to someone qualified.

setup.heading: Set your location
setup.body: Prayer times, the Qibla direction, the Hijri calendar and the salah tracker all need to know where you are. It is computed on your device and never sent anywhere - and you can change it any time from the prayer times screen.

prayerPages.metaTitle: Prayer Times in {city}, {country} | Today's Salah Times
prayerPages.metaDescription: Today in {city}: Fajr {fajr}, Maghrib {maghrib}. Full month of salah times, the Qibla bearing, and the calculation method used.
prayerPages.qiblaBody: From {city}, the Qibla is {bearing} degrees from true north, measured as a great circle to the Kaaba. A phone compass reads magnetic north, which differs from true north by a few degrees in most places, so treat a compass reading as close rather than exact.
prayerPages.methodApproximatedNote: The national authority here uses its own convention, which is not one of the presets available. The nearest equivalent is used, and the result can differ from a local timetable by a minute or two.
prayerPages.assistantPrompt: How do I combine Maghrib and Isha when travelling?
prayerPages.hubIntro: Times, the Qibla bearing and the calculation method for cities around the world, computed rather than fetched.
prayerPages.countryIntro: {count} cities in {country}, each with today's times, the full month, and the Qibla bearing.
prayerPages.countryMetaTitle: Prayer Times in {country} | Salah Times by City
prayerPages.countryMetaDescription: Salah times for cities across {country}, with the Qibla bearing and the calculation method used in each.

methodWhy.mwl: These use the Muslim World League convention, which sets Fajr at 18 degrees of solar depression and Isha at 17. It is the most widely applied standard in {country} and across Europe generally, and it is what most mosques there follow.
methodWhy.isna: These use the ISNA convention, 15 degrees for both Fajr and Isha. It is the standard most mosques in {country} follow, and the shallower angle produces noticeably later Fajr and earlier Isha than the European standards at the same latitude.
methodWhy.umm_al_qura: These use Umm al-Qura, the convention of the Two Holy Mosques and the standard throughout {country}. Fajr is set at 18.5 degrees, and Isha is fixed at 90 minutes after Maghrib rather than by a solar angle.
methodWhy.karachi: These use the University of Islamic Sciences in Karachi convention, 18 degrees for both Fajr and Isha. It is the standard across {country} and the wider subcontinent.
methodWhy.egyptian: These use the Egyptian General Authority of Survey convention, 19.5 degrees for Fajr and 17.5 for Isha. It is the standard in {country} and much of the region.
methodWhy.moonsighting: These use the Moonsighting Committee method, which adjusts the twilight angle by season and latitude rather than holding it fixed.

extremeLatitude.heading: This far north, the sun does not cooperate
extremeLatitude.body: {city} sits at {latitude} degrees. The longest day of the year runs to about {longest} hours and the shortest to about {shortest}, so for part of the summer true astronomical twilight never ends and Fajr and Isha cannot be determined by solar angle at all. The times here use the nearest-latitude rule, which borrows the pattern from the last date the angles were reachable. Local mosques may use a different rule, and where they do, theirs governs.

highLatitude.heading: Why Fajr moves so much here
highLatitude.body: {city} is at {latitude} degrees, far enough north that the gap between the earliest and latest Fajr across the year is about {spreadHours} hours. Fajr reaches {earliestFajr} at midsummer while Isha does not fall until {latestIsha}, which leaves a very short night. This is a property of the latitude rather than of the calculation, and it is why the summer months are demanding here in a way they are not nearer the equator.

equatorial.heading: Times barely move here
equatorial.body: {city} is at {latitude} degrees, close enough to the equator that day length varies by only about {rangeMinutes} minutes across the entire year. Prayer times shift by a few minutes between seasons and little more, so a timetable printed in January is still broadly right in July.

moderateVariation.heading: Across the year
moderateVariation.body: In {city} Fajr ranges from {earliestFajr} at the height of summer to {latestFajr} in deep winter, a spread of about {spreadMinutes} minutes. The shift is gradual, a minute or so every few days, which is why a monthly table is more useful than a single day's figures.

southernSeasons.heading: Southern hemisphere
southernSeasons.body: The seasons here run opposite to most published guidance on prayer times, which is written from a northern perspective. The longest days fall in December and January, and Ramadan moves through the seasons in the reverse direction to how it is usually described.

methodApproximated.heading: About the local authority
methodApproximated.body: The national religious authority here publishes its own timetable using a convention of its own. The figures on this page are computed with the closest standard convention and will normally agree to within a minute or two, but where they differ, the local timetable is the one to follow.

ummAlQuraIsha.heading: Isha is fixed, not calculated
ummAlQuraIsha.body: Under Umm al-Qura, Isha is not derived from a solar angle. It is set at 90 minutes after Maghrib for most of the year and 120 minutes during Ramadan. That is why Isha here moves in step with sunset rather than drifting against it as it does under angle-based conventions.

hanafiAsr.heading: A note on Asr
hanafiAsr.body: The Asr on this page uses the majority position, where the shadow of an object equals its own length plus the noon shadow. The Hanafi school, which is followed by most Muslims in this region, waits until the shadow is twice that length, which typically falls between forty minutes and an hour and a half later. If your mosque prays Asr noticeably later than shown here, this is usually why.

tomorrowFajr.q: What time is Fajr in {city} tomorrow?
tomorrowFajr.a: Fajr is at {tomorrowFajr} tomorrow in {city}, computed for the city's own timezone.

todayIsha.q: What time is Isha in {city} today?
todayIsha.a: Isha is at {isha} today. Today's Fajr was {fajr}.

qiblaDirection.q: Which direction is the Qibla from {city}?
qiblaDirection.a: {bearing} degrees from true north. A phone compass shows magnetic north, which is a few degrees off true north in most places.

methodUsed.q: Which calculation method is used for {city}?
methodUsed.a: {method}. It is the convention most widely followed locally, and the section above explains what it sets.

summerFajr.q: Why is Fajr so early in {city} in summer?
summerFajr.a: The latitude. The sun dips only briefly below the horizon in midsummer, so the angle that defines Fajr is reached very soon after Isha. It is a property of where the city is, not of the method.

winterIsha.q: Why is Isha so early in {city} in winter?
winterIsha.a: Short winter days mean the sun sets early and reaches the Isha angle soon after. Maghrib and Isha can fall within about an hour of each other at midwinter.

errorPage.heading: Something went wrong
errorPage.body: This page failed to load. It has been reported, so we know about it. Trying again often works, because most of these are momentary.

about.intro: What it draws on, what it refuses to do, and why a question of Islamic law is treated differently from everything else.
